title: Rust Project and Final Review
subtitle: A short practical refresher followed by 20 new application questions
description: Review the ten Rust dashboard topics. Includes three capstone examples and exactly two fresh review questions from each of Lessons 1–10.

blocks.text: Welcome to the Rust final review. This lesson is intentionally shorter on new theory and longer on practical decisions. You will revisit the ten dashboard topics and answer two new application questions for each lesson, for exactly 20 questions.

Start by reading the requirement, tracing where its data comes from, and deciding what success should look like. Then test both a normal case and a boundary or failure case. A correct program should not only work once; it should behave predictably when its inputs change.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select Rust. Paste this snippet into the Rust editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 1: Rust Project and Final Review
blocks.code: fn main() { let scores = [72, 86, 91]; let total: i32 = scores.iter().sum(); println!("Average: {:.1}", total as f64 / scores.len() as f64); }

blocks.text: The first sample illustrates a small part of the solution. Before extending it, separate the input, the transformation, and the output. That separation makes it easier to test each part and locate defects.

A final project combines several ideas instead of treating each lesson as an isolated trick. Keep the responsibilities clear, choose data structures that match the job, and validate information at the boundary where it enters the program.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select Rust. Paste this snippet into the Rust editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 2: Rust Project and Final Review
blocks.code: fn main() { let correct = true; let xp = if correct { 5 } else { 0 }; println!("XP earned: {xp}"); }

blocks.text: Now consider how this idea would behave with empty data, invalid input, and a larger set of records. If an operation can fail, design the response deliberately rather than showing a success message before the operation has actually succeeded.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select Rust. Paste this snippet into the Rust editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 3: Rust Project and Final Review
blocks.code: fn main() { let done = 4; let total = 10; println!("Progress: {}%", done * 100 / total); }

blocks.text: Use the third example as a starting point, then explain how it relates to the course topic: Build a structured Rust project while reviewing ownership, borrowing, structs, enums, traits, error handling and concurrency.

Answer two questions from each dashboard lesson. These questions are newly written for this review and are not copied from the corresponding lesson quizzes. Read carefully: select the option that best satisfies the requirement, not merely an option that could work in a different situation.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to Rust: A team receives a repository with no run instructions. What should the maintainer add to make a fresh setup verifiable?
options: A setup/run guide plus a minimal test or sample command.
Only a screenshot of the editor.
A larger logo.
A statement that setup is obvious.
blocks.explanation: A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to Rust: The app works after manual edits but fails when built from source. What should be compared?
options: The wallpaper on each device.
The actual source, compiler/runtime configuration, and documented build path.
The author’s typing speed.
The names of unrelated files.
blocks.explanation: Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 2 — Variables, Mutability and Data Types: Two components disagree about a learner’s current XP. Which refactor is strongest?
options: Keep both independent values and sync them by hand.
Show both values so the user chooses.
Use one authoritative value and derive each display from it.
Store the value in a constant even though it changes.
blocks.explanation: One source of truth avoids state drift.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. One source of truth avoids state drift.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. One source of truth avoids state drift.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 2 — Variables, Mutability and Data Types: A production setting should not change after configuration. How should it be represented?
options: As an input field that always accepts edits.
As duplicated mutable global state.
As a variable reset every second.
As a constant/immutable binding after safe configuration.
blocks.explanation: Immutable configuration communicates that the value should not be reassigned.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Immutable configuration communicates that the value should not be reassigned.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Immutable configuration communicates that the value should not be reassigned.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Functions, Expressions and Control Flow: Two features calculate eligibility differently after one rule changes. What is a better design?
options: Keep both implementations independent.
Put the rule in a comment only.
Share one tested function that owns the eligibility rule.
Let each screen guess.
blocks.explanation: Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Functions, Expressions and Control Flow: A calculation’s output is needed by three later operations. Which interface is most useful?
options: Only print a decorative message.
Return nothing and rely on visible output.
Store the result in an unrelated global.
Return a value with a clear contract.
blocks.explanation: Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 6 — Structs, Enums and Pattern Matching: An object’s internal data can be changed into impossible combinations by any caller. What design improvement addresses that?
options: Encapsulate state and expose validated operations.
Make even more fields public.
Duplicate the object every time.
Remove all types.
blocks.explanation: Encapsulation helps enforce invariants across every caller.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Encapsulation helps enforce invariants across every caller.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Encapsulation helps enforce invariants across every caller.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 6 — Structs, Enums and Pattern Matching: A design uses deep inheritance to share one small helper. What alternative should be evaluated?
options: An even deeper inheritance chain.
Composition or a small interface when the relationship is not truly “is-a.”
Public mutable state everywhere.
No tests of the helper.
blocks.explanation: Composition can reuse behavior without forcing an incorrect type relationship.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Composition can reuse behavior without forcing an incorrect type relationship.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Composition can reuse behavior without forcing an incorrect type relationship.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 7 — Collections, Strings and Error Handling: A collection is used to retrieve a learner by a unique identifier. What design question matters most?
options: Whether a map/dictionary keyed by the identifier fits the lookup requirement and uniqueness rule.
Whether the item names are colorful.
Whether the code has a heading.
Whether every collection uses indexes.
blocks.explanation: Data structures should fit the expected access pattern and identity constraints.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Data structures should fit the expected access pattern and identity constraints.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Data structures should fit the expected access pattern and identity constraints.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 7 — Collections, Strings and Error Handling: A filtered list is unexpectedly missing items after an update. What should you check?
options: Only the page title.
Whether the loop/indexing or collection mutation changes the original values during iteration.
The operating system wallpaper.
Whether comments are uppercase.
blocks.explanation: Collection mutation and index behavior can cause skipped, duplicated, or missing results.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Collection mutation and index behavior can cause skipped, duplicated, or missing results.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Collection mutation and index behavior can cause skipped, duplicated, or missing results.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 9 — Modules, Packages and Concurrency: A service call fails, but the application still shows “Saved successfully.” What needs correction?
options: Use a more colorful success message.
Remove the error path.
Only show success after confirmation and provide meaningful failure handling.
Repeat the same request indefinitely.
blocks.explanation: A success message must reflect confirmed success, and failures need accurate handling.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A success message must reflect confirmed success, and failures need accurate handling.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A success message must reflect confirmed success, and failures need accurate handling.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 9 — Modules, Packages and Concurrency: An input fails numeric parsing. What should the program preserve?
options: An unvalidated value as though it were valid.
A made-up fallback without a documented rule.
No record of the problem.
A clear validation result so it can reject or recover according to the app’s policy.
blocks.explanation: Explicit validation prevents malformed input from contaminating later calculations.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Explicit validation prevents malformed input from contaminating later calculations.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Explicit validation prevents malformed input from contaminating later calculations.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 10 — Rust Project and Final Review: The final project passes one example input. What is the strongest completion check?
options: Stop testing as soon as the screen appears.
Remove error handling to reduce lines.
Test normal, boundary, empty, and failure cases and document how to run it.
Change the app name again.
blocks.explanation: Broader tests and reproducible setup provide stronger evidence than one happy-path example.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Broader tests and reproducible setup provide stronger evidence than one happy-path example.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Broader tests and reproducible setup provide stronger evidence than one happy-path example.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 10 — Rust Project and Final Review: A teammate cannot reproduce the project’s behavior. What is likely missing?
options: A larger icon.
A longer splash screen.
More animated effects.
Repeatable instructions, clear dependencies, and a testable expected result.
blocks.explanation: Reproducibility requires enough source and setup information for another person to verify the same behavior.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Reproducibility requires enough source and setup information for another person to verify the same behavior.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Reproducibility requires enough source and setup information for another person to verify the same behavior.
